inline.s: Two Poems on Leaving Caoxi

To speed the Caoxi's ten-thousand-mile flow,
my heart turns home and strokes the broadsword's hilt.
I think of the snow that bathed his waist in blood —
through a thousand years the grief has never stilled.

I came to Caoxi leaning on my staff,
sat gazing at the hills, my face alight.
Today I leave for a thousand peaks away —
bird calls and stream sounds brim with endless grief.
Two Poems on Rejoicing in Snow, Newly Arrived at Hengyang

The Seventy Peaks are steeped in cold snow;
arriving here, I see this mind at peace.
Remembering the burning house where I once raced —
all now appears within an ice-jar's gleam.

In the five-heat realm a phantom body born,
for twenty years I drifted with the dust.
Today I come to the snows of Xiang —
of old, a man whose very bones were cool.
Twenty-Eight Poems on Dwelling in the Mountains

All my life I have held a passion for mist and cloud. In my early years I wandered on foot; at thirty I lived eight years among the ice and snow of Mount Wutai, and afterward dwelt twelve years by the Eastern Sea. In the year I knew my fate, the wind of karma blew me down into the land of miasma, and there nearly twenty years passed. Alas, how much is a human life? In the blink of an eye I have come and gone and am already seventy. Floating light and phantom shadow — how could they last? Lately, by the grace of His Majesty, I was granted return to my former station, and I came of purpose to the Southern Marchmount to make plans for my old age. The causes were not yet ripe, so I settled at the old Way-site east of the lake. Relying on the help of the benefactors, I built a dwelling for retreat. It was begun on the sixteenth day of the ninth month of the jia-yin year and finished by the very last days of the twelfth month — roughly completed in haste. From this time on, body and mind at last have a place of rest, like a long-wandering guest come home, setting down a heavy burden. What joy could match such ease and freedom? At once I chanted verses and had my attendant write them down, to record my hidden feelings — these are no crafted poems. When the mood came I took up the brush, with no order at all.

In Jetavana I borrowed a branch to rest;
from now I need not speak of roads made hard.
The sun is three poles high and still I lie —
no need for anyone to urge me to eat more.

Snow weighs the wicket gate; at night I hug the stove.
This body is lodged here, yet seems to be nowhere.
I do not know where sun and moon have gone;
looking back, the years of the world have passed away.

A little hut amid the tangled brush,
a stone for seat, the grasses for its shrine.
Shut in, I seem a Vimalakīrti;
ask nothing of three before or three behind.

My form a withered tree, my thoughts like ash,
snow on my crown and frost upon my cheeks.
It is not that in age I shun the world —
these eyes have nowhere left to set down dust.

Body and mind set down, I have spare ease;
my late-year life lies in ten thousand hills.
I will not let white clouds slip lightly from the vale —
let them keep the moon and guard my brushwood gate.

A cold lamp shines alone, my shadow faint;
through a sparse roof the wind blows snow across my robe.
Suddenly I recall where I sat cross-legged on Wutai —
a single brushwood door amid ten-thousand-year ice.

Cold pierces to the bone, snow on a thousand peaks;
rage buffets the man, wind through ten thousand hollows.
Wrapped head and all beneath my quilt, just woken from sleep,
I do not know this body is in the midst of stillness.

A hundred thousand worlds are shadows of a flower in air;
this body and mind the light of moon in water.
When every trick is spent, all tidings cease —
within it there is nowhere to set a thought.

The earth-stove has no fire, the stone bed is cold;
in the earthen censer the incense dies as night wears on.
Every sound of the world sinks still, the mind more still —
yet I half wonder I am gazing from within a mirror.

Cold rain falls sighing, wind fills the wood;
the lotus water-clock runs long, the night is deep.
Who knows the whole world cannot wake from its dream?
All of it is the bright light of prajñā's heart.

Deep in the night I sit alone at dry-pith Chan;
I rake the cold ash through, the fire will not catch.
Then suddenly the bell and chime sound from the tower —
one clear note fills the frosty sky.

Snow fills the world, ten thousand forms made new;
I hide myself inside a world of silver.
Sitting, I suddenly enter the storehouse of light —
and this place has never held one speck of dust.

The level lake soaks cold the garb of water-caltrop and lotus;
the blue hills above the lake are free of right and wrong.
All worldly traces melt, the human world falls far —
white clouds and gulls have both forgotten schemes.

When snow heaps at the brushwood door and I sit alone,
inch by inch the cold wood snaps its jade-like boughs.
At dawn the blue hills' color has suddenly vanished —
the plum has blossomed out and I never knew.

Spring passes, the Day of Man is gone, the snow first clears;
the new moon through sparse woods casts shadows all the clearer.
At night I rise and push the window open to the vastness —
the whole sky's stars hang from the eaves and pillars.

The clouds draw back, spring light stirs across four wilds;
from where does plum send its secret fragrance?
Staff in hand, I would go seek the hidden vale —
one branch leans aslant by the eastern wall.

A single cloud seals the pines of ten thousand ravines;
before my door the stream goes babbling day by day.
It cares not night or day, but serves my snoring sleep —
fair dreams are startled back by a bell beyond the ridge.

Deep spring, the rain has passed, the fallen blossoms fly;
softly heavenly fragrance climbs onto my robe.
A single idle heart that has nowhere to settle —
at the peak's edge I lean on my staff and watch the clouds go home.

Strolling at ease, I let my steps go where they will;
this frame of mine is like a pine in snow.
By chance I come and stand a while at the stream's head,
then follow the idle clouds across another peak

In the empty hills with deer, whom should I follow?
I will yield to the lush grass and the tall pines.
Though the red dust holds dreams hard to wake from,
the world-cutting man has never reached these myriad peaks.

Hanging white hair faces the blue hills;
this body dwells among a thousand cliffs and ten thousand gorges.
The pine gate is still, no passing guest comes by —
only white clouds wander to and fro at ease.

The blue hills do not move, thusness as it is;
morning and evening the cloud-mist rolls and spreads at will.
Though the red dust lie ten thousand fathoms deep,
not one speck has ever reached my thatched hut.

Deep among ten thousand peaks I sit cross-legged alone;
clear and distinct, the void-bright single thought stands solitary.
This body is like the bright moon hung in cold space —
only its clear shadow remains, fallen on rivers and lakes.

Waking from sleep I call the boy to brew tea;
the bamboo stove boils up, its froth like snowflakes.
Before the leaf unfurls, Māra has already withdrawn —
now I believe the groves hold true masters still.

Weary, I lean at the empty window, sitting to watch the hills;
a thousand peaks of purple and green rise from the pines.
My mind makes no claim, so let the clouds come and go —
how much more at ease is the thusness of my own being.

Moonlight and the sound of pines are all seen and heard;
the Chan mind and idle thoughts divide the sage from the common.
Melt them back to the single thought where nothing is born —
how shall I put this meaning into words for you?

Autumn water on the level lake soaks the cold sky;
old trees shed frost, red leaves fall.
On the stone path and little bridge all human tracks are cut —
a single hut is locked deep within the white clouds.
Sent to the Old Monk of Shun Hermitage
Sent to Wei Kaoshu

In quiet seclusion, just like a monk who stays at home;
one room as clear as ice in the sixth month.
Though you master emptiness and all that is comes to an end,
mountains and waters still hang upon your brow.
Written on Parting from the Friends of the East-of-the-Lake Society

The udumbara hall stands west of the bamboo grove;
far from the market's clamor, it is the best of dwellings.
Sweep the cloud-strewn ground before the steps with care —
when I return, do not let the grass run wild.

By chance I came beneath the pines and closed the brushwood gate;
you summoned the recluse to seek the world beyond.
How could I think I would drift off with the flowing water?
In parting from you my heart clings to the clouded hills.
Two Poems, Held by Wind at Yueyang

Beyond Yueyang Tower the lake soaks into the sky;
below the tower a sandbar, a boat moored for the night.
Wind-borne sails come and go, and none can be detained —
only the hills' color remains as it always was.

North wind drives the waves to beat the mountain town;
a single light sail is held back from its course.
I think it means to keep me here to watch Dongting's moon —
no wonder it shines so bright toward a traveler's side.
Passing the Cloud Grove of Yu Runfu at Jinsha

The Cloud Grove is close at hand, not far to see;
arriving, the cold air is crisp and clear.
The gate is shut and will not let the mist and cloud out —
how many a worldly thought here fades away.
Written at Random on West Lake

Hills and lake on every side, seen as in a mirror;
the great boats sink deep in the cold green waves.
I do not know this body lies within an ice-jar's shadow —
laughable, to be deep drunk with a dream not yet ended.
Mourning Master Chekong of Yellow Dragon, Mount Kuang

Formerly I dwelt with the Master amid the ice and snow of Mount Wutai for three years. Since we parted, more than thirty years have passed. Now I have come to Mount Kuang to spend my old age. I bowed once at the Master's stupa and mourned him with these poems.

I recall the days we sat facing each other at Qingliang;
hoar-frost and snow hung heavy on both our brows.
Since we parted, my dreams reach the place that breaks the heart —
a grief I cannot hold back, known only to myself.

The stupa's round shadow is embraced by ten thousand pines;
the dharma-body does not move, towering over a thousand peaks.
I know the Master always taught the Dharma of no-birth —
bird calls and stream sounds join the morning bell.
A Snowy Night in the Mountains

Snow hems a thousand peaks, I shut the gate alone;
a cold lamp in deep night lights this aging face.
The mind's ash has died out, red-dust dreams cut off —
who would believe the world holds such leisure as this?
Written on Waking from a Dream While Reading the Ten Stages Chapter of the Avatamsaka Sutra

A single leaf of a light boat and a single fishing rod;
the fragrant bait on the hook has never yet been nibbled.
You must plunge into the sea and seize your catch deep down —
do not linger on the shallow shoals among the reeds.
Two Songs of Homesickness
I left my home village at the age of twelve. Now it is sixty years. It happened that a man of my village sent word asking after me in the mountains, and so I wrote these.

Tall willows before the gate mirrored in the clear pool;
I always remember the children at play in the water.
More than sixty years, a thing like a dream —
how many times it still stirs my longing for the old garden.

A belt of blue hills winds around the river;
my home stood by the old ferry on the bank.
I left the village young and now am old —
this heart runs on unbroken as the endless water.
Thinking of the Master of Longhua in the Great Capital

Beneath the Longhua tree, a man of karmic bond;
since we parted, no one matches the closeness we once had.
How many times my dream-soul has flown to the night moon —
even if we met, it would never be real.
Entering the Mountains

Straight into a thousand peaks, never weary of the depth;
in the most secluded, uttermost place the mind can rest.
Let the pine gate gather moss as thick as it will —
from now on the people of the world will find no way to seek me.
Two Poems in Reply to Venerable Fu Wu'ang, Master of the Caoxi Hall

Since I left Caoxi, ten springs have passed;
I often long for one sip of its fragrant water.
In dreams my soul still sits beneath the pine shade —
I only fear this life is a later body still.

By the stream the plum's fragrance never fails;
how often its scented mist has damped my robe.
In recent years, whenever I come to a place to view the blossoms,
it is just as when I once sat in the Dharma Hall.
Seeing Off Master Xi of Green Forest on His Journey to the Southern Marchmount

I recall how I once climbed the Seventy Peaks,
leaning on heaven, companion to the sun, stroking the tall pines.
Through hidden crags and sheer ravines I searched out every wonder —
go now and seek the tracks my staff once left.

Deep among ten thousand peaks the green clouds are cold;
there I once built a thatched hut and studied Lazy Repose.
The fire for roasting taro is still buried in cow dung —
go stir the earthen stove and see for yourself.
Written at Random

The limpid sea, its waves becalmed, holds not one thing;
in the cold sky deep night, the moon's wheel stands alone.
Just see the ten thousand miles where not a wisp of cloud remains —
you will know your own ice-clear heart within its jade jar.
Rejoicing That My Old Mother Has Sent My Brother to Me

Kin of one blood take pity, sharing a single stem;
the lord's grace has granted me one body back.
If a day of living return should come at last,
I may still wait upon my kind mother.
Remembering My Old Home

My home stood on the shady side of Turtle Hill,
just like a bend along the Ganges.
And I remember, as a child,
how hot we were, bathing in the river.

On either bank the willow shade was thick;
at the door the southern hills were green.
With my own hands I planted a green-blossomed peach —
I do not know if it is still there.

Before the gate there was a little bridge;
as a child I saw the water wash it out.
I wanted to frame it with a single log;
the road was far and it was never done.
Remembering Friends of My Village

When we were small we studied together,
sharing one bed and one quilt.
Who would have thought that once we parted,
in a blink we would be sixty years old?

And I remember when we piled up sand,
our games together always ending in a quarrel.
I recall only a boy's face —
I cannot believe the two of us are old now.
Remembering the Hermitage in My Home Hills

My storied dwelling joined the water and the bamboo;
through long summer, clear breeze and sleep in broad daylight.
Today, beyond ten thousand miles of burning wilds,
looking back, it seems a life or two ago.
The Dream-Journey Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Fifty

blocks.text: Record of the Revival of Caoxi

inline.s: Recorded day by day by the bodhisattva-precept disciple, the monk Ben'ang, Feng Changli, and the monk Zhirong
Compiled by the official disciples Wang Anshun and Liu Qixiang
Collated by the Changchun Society disciples Chen Dixiang and Liang Sixiang
Record of the Revival of Caoxi, Part One
The Causes of the Revival

The Master said: Caoxi takes its name from Cao Shuliang of old, a descendant of Emperor Wu of Wei, who took refuge here. Its Way-site begins with the holy monk Tripiṭaka Master Jñānaphala of Liang, who came by sea from the Western Heaven and brought a bodhi tree to the Faxing Monastery of Wuyang. His prophecy ran: “In one hundred and sixty years a bodhisattva in the flesh will leave home here and save countless beings.” As he came into the range he passed the mouth of the Caoxi stream, scooped up water and drank; it was sweet and fragrant. “This is the water of my Western Heaven,” he said. “Above its source there must be a holy place.” So he followed the stream up and viewed its mountain, which looked like an elephant. “This mountain is just like Bīn-lin Mountain in my Western Heaven,” he said, and told the resident Cao Shuliang: “A monastery should be built on this mountain. In one hundred and sixty years a bodhisattva in the flesh will preach the Dharma here.” Shuliang reported it to the provincial governor, who memorialized the throne, and Emperor Wu of Liang ordered a monastery built with the plaque Baolin — this was the beginning of the mountain's founding.

In the Longshuo period of the Tang there was an adept named Lu of Xinzhou who received the robe and bowl of Huangmei and was known as the Sixth Patriarch. He returned to Caoxi, but by then Baolin had fallen into ruin. A nun named Wujin met the Sixth Patriarch and questioned him on the meaning of the Nirvāṇa Sutra; recognizing him as no ordinary man, she told her father and brothers, and they rebuilt Baolin and invited the Patriarch to dwell there. Before long someone plotted against the Patriarch; he fled for safety to Huai and Hui and hid among a band of hunters for fifteen years. Later he came to the Faxing Monastery in Wuyang, where his worth showed itself; he had his head shaved beneath the bodhi tree and returned at once to Caoxi, opening the Dharma at Baolin. By then the mountain had changed owners and belonged to the Chen family. The Patriarch taught for many years and great crowds gathered. Because the mountain is like a living elephant with tusks and trunk complete, the first monastery stood inside the great tusk of the left jaw, while the trunk lies to the right, where the ancestral graves of the Chen family already were, so the temple site was very cramped. One day the Patriarch asked the resident Chen Yaxian for the ground of one sitting-mat. Yaxian agreed, and when the Patriarch spread his mat it covered all the ridges of the four mountains. Then the Four Heavenly Kings appeared at the four corners, and Yaxian at once consented, saying: “I know the Master's Dharma-power is vast; I shall give it all. But my forebears' graves lie to the right of the temple; when you build in days to come, I beg you to keep them.” He added: “The form of this mountain is the coming vein of a living dragon and white elephant. When you build hereafter, you may level only what touches the sky, never the ground.” Then Yaxian took his family and withdrew into hiding; where he went is unknown. Thus from the time the Sixth Patriarch founded this mountain, all within the Four Heavenly Kings' ring, some tens of miles around, was one monastery, with no dwellings of laypeople. The mountain's form and its wind and air were whole and dense; even among all the ancestral Way-sites of the patriarchs from Shaolin onward, none could match its excellence. Monks always treated it as a place of hidden cultivation. Down to the beginning of our dynasty, when fields were opened, all within the ring of mountains became farmland entered on the tax registers, so monks took farming as their basic livelihood, planting, grafting, and breeding, no different from laymen. Yet there had never been lay dwellings there. In the Hongzhi and Zhengde reigns, drifters from every quarter gradually gathered in the mountains. At first they hired themselves out; in time they set up in business with capital borrowed from the monks, and the monks did not notice. Since the mountain gate led to Wengyuan and was a main road into the prefecture, the drifters gradually made it a den, spread along the roadside and opened shops and stalls. Was this only magpies seizing the magpie's nest? It would soon be wolves squatting in the lion's cave. The monks too abandoned the temple and lived on the estates, so the mountain gate grew emptier by day, the drifters gathered by day, and harm arose by day, until the monks were caught in these entanglements and could barely preserve the place at all.

In the spring of the bing-shen year I was graced with exile beyond the range. When first I entered the mountains to bow to the Patriarch, I saw how ruinous and unbearable things had become; before long the disaster indeed broke out and the monks were scattered. At once those in authority hastened to rescue the situation. At first the Commander-in-Chief Lord Chen wished me to go and set it right; before that could happen, the Surveillance Commissioner Lord Zhou of Haimen, who had great concern for the ancestral Way, was already at work on it, and presently left to offer congratulations. The Circuit Commissioner Lord Zhu then urged me most earnestly. Thereupon certain monks of the temple came one after another to take refuge, asked to receive the full precepts, and pressed their request with firm resolve; I consented. In the ninth month of the autumn of the geng-zi year I entered the mountains and took the ancestral courtyard to heart. I staked body and life on it, ordering each matter one by one and establishing them in due sequence, as listed below. In sum, all was a shattered ruin beyond repair, not to be endured a single day. Happily, relying on the spirit of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and the protection of the Dharma by those in authority, with unseen divine aid, in eight years some order was achieved. Though the work was not brought to final completion, my heart and strength were utterly spent. What was built can all serve as lasting rule; if the monks can from now on keep it carefully and not lose it, this Way-site may be preserved and be free of care for generation after generation. At that time the Master directed Changli and the others to remain in the temple to instruct the novices; everything done was witnessed by them, and every word spoken was recorded the same day. In time it became a volume, entitled Veritable Record of the Revival, following the pattern of the ten chapters of the Tongxin and arranged in ten sections; his instructions to the assembly, the pure rules, his letters, and miscellaneous writings are set out in order after them.
Nurturing the Ancestral Dragon to Complete the Site's Fengshui

When the Master first entered the mountains and saw the ancestral courtyard in ruin, he gathered his disciples and said: The Buddha taught that the great earth and its mountains and rivers are fused and formed by the One Mind alone. Though the words of geomancers are not all to be trusted, the highest principle is present in them. When Yaxian first gave up the land he said that this mountain was the coming vein of a living dragon and white elephant, and that in building hereafter one might level only what touches the sky, never the ground. This means the lie of the land must not be injured. Look at the host mountain of Caoxi: it is plainly shaped like an elephant, with four feet and six tusks, trunk and mouth complete. When Baolin was first founded the mountain's form was whole and dense, so the temple sat within the jaw, wrapped by the great tusk on the left and joined with the tusk on the right. Inside the lips was the Dragon Pool, which is the elephant's mouth. The right wall of Baolin is plainly the elephant's trunk, and the ancestral grave of Chen Yaxian was buried upon it first. In the Sixth Patriarch's day it stood just outside the Baolin wall — hence he asked for that ground and enlarged the site. The mouth is the Dragon Pool, where water gathered and a dragon dwelled. When the Patriarch subdued that dragon he cut through the point where the two tusks meet, drained the water and filled the pool in order to raise the Buddha Hall. But once the dragon had shed its form and the water was gone, the sacred energy leaked away; the Buddha Hall was complete, yet the pool was never fully filled when the Patriarch passed into stillness. To this day the space before the hall is still a deep pit — an unfinished work from former days. Thus the altar terrace reached only halfway. The Master understood the cause and filled it level. The former Arhat Tower stands where the ridge was first cut through; later men made it the mountain gate, and in time built a tower above. The Master wished to alter and repair it but had not the time. The elephant's feeding depends on its trunk, and its life lies in the trunk; the trunk should have several joints, and the Chen grave lies right at its center. So when the Sixth Patriarch entered nirvāṇa, his preserved body was first placed in a wooden pagoda built before the grave for offerings, and behind the grave the Faith-Offering Pavilion was built to house the robe and bowl. In the Chenghua period of our Ming, a certain monk removed the wooden pagoda and replaced it with brick; the interior was damp and dark, and before long the Patriarch appeared in a dream to the prefect, asking for a lodging. The prefect ordered the Faith-Offering Pavilion changed into the Patriarch's Hall, and the empty pagoda left in front became a lump of obstruction in the site's breast. Behind the Patriarch's Hall was the Cheng-Su Pavilion, built in the bing-wu year of Jiajing by the prefect Chen Baogu. When the Master arrived he saw the abbot's quarters to the left of the hall, with a path cut straight through the middle into the back mountain, slicing the elephant's trunk; and behind the hall the ground was low, prey to the north wind, so the incoming vein was injured. This was the very cause of the Way-site's decline. Examining the shape of the elephant's trunk, the Master reckoned that behind the hall there ought to be a high mound. Then an old monk told him: when I was first a novice I saw a heap behind the hall like a piled mound; when Lord Chen built the pavilion he had the monks scrape it away, and I, then a novice, was among those carrying off the earth. The Master knew this was true, so he had the monks selected as instructors in the Three Studies lead more than a hundred novices in their studies to carry ten loads of earth each day to bank it up. In three months a hill was made, as though it had always been there. Then he moved the central path to the side of the Caoxi and made it a winding corridor that curves right around the ancestral courtyard and leads into the back mountain. Only then was the site's fengshui whole. Within the mountain gate he removed every inauspicious feature, and the monks were at peace. Behind the ancestral hall there is a ravine crossed by the Flying-Tin Bridge; past the bridge is the Staff-Planting Spring, the elephant's throat. The Master led that spring into the incense kitchen. To the right of the spring a small ridge is shaped like a tongue, and right of that a hollow like a clamp — the right jaw. In old times this was the hermitage where the nun Wujin lived, she who was the chief patron of Baolin's revival; so when the Master restored the tradition he rebuilt it first of all. This was the very beginning of his work on entering the mountains.
Renewing the Ancestral Courtyard to Inspire Reverence

The ancestral courtyard was at first made by converting the Faith-Offering Pavilion, and it was exceedingly mean and cramped. Entering the gate, one could not make out the Patriarch's countenance; there was no room to array the rows for worship. In front, moreover, a worship hall joined its eaves to the roof, making it very dark. A pagoda stood tall before the grave, and beyond the pagoda the halls of the gods were layered upon one another, broken and patched together, so that at the very front there was not a crack of open ground. Near the left of the hall were monks' rooms, huddled like a fist propping up a chin; at the lower right was the household chief's kitchen, heaped with filth. The monks' quarters on either flank had sagging beams, like a thicket of thorns. Seen from outside, the buildings were jagged and gaping, with not one clear line of sight through. This is why the ancestral Way was blocked and could not flow freely. The Master saw deeply how hard it would be to open the place up; he thought day and night, yet could devise no plan to make a coherent whole. Often he climbed the pagoda and gazed out, carefully observing the whole temple's layout. To the left were the abbot's quarters, the Dharma Hall, and the Chan Hall; in front stood the bell and drum towers, flanking it into one unit. The Master said: this must have been the original arrangement when Baolin was first founded. To the right was the Buddha Hall, which the Patriarch built by filling the Dragon Pool in his own day; behind it the sutra pavilion, in front the Arhat Tower, and the Baolin mountain gate, all forming one unit. Later men made poor additions, so the Patriarch's Hall ended up in the middle with monks' quarters mixed in around it, choking the spirit path and leaving no air of reverence at all. Now, if one would sort it out thread by thread and give it a proper plan, what hand but a giant spirit's could cleave it apart?

So seeing that the hill west of the Arhat Tower was like a tiger turning its head to look back, the Master bought that hill and took its earth to fill the pool-pit before the great hall, raising the ground so as to move the monks' quarters left of the Patriarch's Hall. He also bought other houses to exchange for the monks' rooms behind the sutra pavilion, making them into public offices for the household chief, and so removed the filth at the western corner of the Patriarch's Hall. The monks of the two corridors were each given separate dwellings. The halls of the gods and the worship hall in front were demolished, and at once the ground before one was level as a palm. Then he threw himself into the work with all his strength, and everything came out as he had pictured it. So he was able to rebuild the Patriarch's Hall, lofty and fair to see, with two side halls before it to enshrine the images of the five schools from Nanyue and Qingyuan. The gate house had fifteen bays around it, meant to enshrine the patriarchs of the Lamp Transmission and their descendants, like the seventy disciples offered sacrifice alongside Confucius. But the path in front was still choked, so he bought open ground and moved three monks' quarters that stood in the way, opening a great spirit path that runs level with the Baolin gate and abreast of the Arhat Tower. He raised a three-bay Avatamsaka Tower as the head gate of the ancestral courtyard, and above it a Chan Hall where the monks copy the Avatamsaka Sutra. Thus, naturally, it became a noble prospect. Visitors today see only that all is clear at a glance, and do not know how hard the opening up of it was to accomplish.
Selecting Monks of Conduct to Nurture Talent

The monks of this temple had long been at ease living on the estates, planting and breeding, no different from laymen. Of the temple's hundred quarters, every door was barred, and once inside the gate not a soul was to be seen — only a few monks tending the incense at the Patriarch's Hall and a few in the abbot's quarters. Thus drifters ran wild at the mountain gate while the monks came and went hiding their shadows and covering their tracks. It was hateful. When the Master first arrived, he put the nurturing of talent first. He selected the whole temple's monks: those over forty were left to their own convenience; those under forty and over twenty, one or two from each quarter, were to dwell in the temple at peace, going up to the halls every day and reciting the four daily liturgies to pray for the Emperor's long life, and those who failed were fined in varying degrees. Thus more than a hundred monks gathered, and all were given the precepts. From then on bells and drums sounded at dawn and dusk, and the sound of sutras continued unbroken — a noble Way-site indeed. The monks came to know they had a proper calling, and outside insults gradually learned caution. But the monks' habits had become the custom; when a young boy left home he saw only his teacher busy with farming, no different from a layman, and never knew what the monastic calling was. Those who raised disciples sought only their usefulness in the fields, and not one word was ever said of what lies beyond the world. This had gone on so long that to hope for men of worth was impossible. At the very start of his time in the temple the Master chose from the assembly those of learning fit to be teachers — Ben'ang and two others — and urged all the monks that any novices under twenty and above eight should report their names to the abbot and be gathered in the temple; three study halls were set up with three instructors to teach the scriptures. Within a year, those who could handle two of the daily liturgies were then taught by Confucian scholars — the licentiate Feng Changli and the talented youths Long Zhang and Liang Sixiang — in the Four Books, expounding their principles and meaning. Their tuition and provisions the Master supplied himself. Thus after three years those who succeeded were shaved and ordained as monks and entered the Chan Hall to learn the rules of the monastic life, each to have his own work in cultivation, recitation, and copying the scriptures. The monks now in the Chan Hall are all talents the Master nurtured. He also said: what the Buddhadharma values is that perfuming and hearing become seeds. Lingnan had long lacked the perfuming of the Buddhadharma, and for want of seeds faith was hard to arouse. So he first had the newly ordained novices copy the great Avatamsaka Sutra: first, because the Dharma-connection is vast and makes the supreme seed; second, because the power of concentration in copying supports the beginner's contemplation and aids the provisions for entering the Way. At first there were two or three; soon everyone looked to one another and brought forth the resolve. Within ten years those who copied this sutra had completed more than ten sets. Such was the Master's work of making people — plainly evident.
Driving Out the Drifters to Wash Away the Stench and Filth

The Master saw that the ruin of the Caoxi Way-site was because drifters from every quarter had gathered in the mountains for more than a hundred years, entrenched beyond dislodging, while laymen's graves filled the valleys and were treated as their own property. It began with hired labor; in time they set up in business, borrowing capital from the monks, and outside the mountain gate they built houses and opened shops — butchery, wine-selling, gambling, and lewdness — and the harm grew daily. Yet the foolish monks did not notice, but grew intimate with them and wormed their way into their favor, each profiting from the other, so that much of what the monks raised fell into their hands. As the gnawing went deeper they turned to lawless schemes, luring men with many devices and setting wine and lust as pits and snares. Once the blind fell in, they were devoured at will and their fat and grease quite drained. Thus many of the monks' fields, mountain lands, and houses were forfeited on this account. Lately the local strongmen too cast greedy eyes that way, colluded with the yamen ruffians, and schemed together; under the pretext of harboring villains they laid accusations before the prefecture and the circuit, using it as a handle to work their swindle, alarming their superiors and shocking their hearing, until it was taken for truth. Then a petition was sent up to the military headquarters, and the order came down that the estates were all to be demolished and monks who broke the rules driven out. The men who received the order were without conscience; trusting their informants, they took it as a windfall. They came into the mountains in person to survey, and at every estate they appraised its full value, so that half had to be paid before one escaped. Thus the temple monks all fell into the net and had already lost half, while the harm was still spreading, with not a moment's peace. In the second year after the Master crossed the range, the ding-you year, he first paid his respects to the Commander-in-Chief Lord Chen and was able to lay out the monks' situation in general, whereupon the order was stayed and they were fortunate to escape. Lord Chen wished at once to send the Master to set matters right, but as he was still in mourning seclusion he did not presume to accept. The next year, wu-xu, Lord Zhou of the Salt and Grain Circuit, acting for Nan-Shao, wished to rescue the situation and asked the Master to compile a gazetteer; before long he left to offer congratulations. In ji-hai, Lord Zhu of the Nan-Shao Circuit took up his post, calling himself a wandering monk of Caoxi; grieving deeply over these abuses, he urged the Master with all his strength to set them in order. In the geng-zi year, Lord Zhu too left to offer congratulations, and on the eve of his departure gave his instructions face to face and had the temple monks earnestly invite the Master to accept the charge. So in the ninth month he entered the mountains. Seeing these men running wild, he knew they were the disease at the very heart of the ancestral courtyard: unless cured, the Sixth Patriarch's wisdom-life could never be saved. So, using the occasion of adjusting the fengshui, he blocked off the great road at the mountain gate to east and west and moved it to the streamside, running straight to the water mouth as the thoroughfare. In this way the former shops and inns were all enclosed inside the mountain gate, and travelers found food and lodging inconvenient. Yet in the end there was no means to remove them.

After three months, at the year's end, he went to pay his respects to the Commander-in-Chief Lord Dai and laid out the whole story of the harm. Lord Dai said: this is the duty of a Dharma-protector. Simply issue one order and charge the local authorities to enforce it strictly; this is the business of a single constable. On New Year's day the order went to the county, which sat watch and drove them out, not leaving a single man; the shops were all demolished, not one tile left. Thus the stench and filth gathered at the mountain gate over more than a hundred years was washed away in a single morning, and the monks' calamity was ended forever. Once the shops were torn down, the market street stood empty. The Master then took the western street, where the butchers had been, and built the Pilgrims' Hall to receive the pilgrims of the ten directions who come to bow to the Patriarch, and on the eastern street built an official residence as a resting place for the Wengyuan magistrates entering the prefecture. The road at the mountain gate had first been a single line, with shops ranged along the left all the way to the very center; he demolished them all. The stone archway, which had stood above, was moved to the streamside. He opened up the blockage so that the two sides faced each other straight as a plumb line, and it became a grand sight. The sources of harm cannot all be told, and their roots ran deep and were hard to pull out; that they were ended in a single morning is summed up here to serve those who come after as a mirror of warning.
Restoring the Properties to Settle the Monks

Once the drifters were driven out, the Master considered that the fields, mountain lands, and houses they had swindled away were all held by deeds in their possession, and that these people, clinging to them, would never let the matter rest. He judged this no sound long-term plan for the aftermath. So he spread a feast in the Patriarch's Hall and invited all the parties, hosts and guests alike, to bring out their deeds and set them side by side. Where the original principal had not yet been covered by interest, he compensated them; where the interest had passed half, the matter was closed; where the principal had already been recovered and only heavy interest remained, or where the account was mere empty talk of food and drink, the claim was dismissed. Then he burned all the deeds, and the fields, mountain lands, and houses all returned to their former owners. From this the outer troubles were ended, and the monks burdened with poverty could dwell in peace, unmolested. Some at the time feared the Master would take the resentment on himself. The Master said: Not so. However bad a man may be, he must have the goodness of his original heart. If matters are made clear and plain, each man knows his own fault for himself, and there is none who will not submit in his heart. So the ruffians gradually withdrew, and in the end there was no further trouble.
Enforcing Fasting and Precepts to Encourage Pure Practice

Formerly many of the temple monks did not keep the fasts and precepts, but bred and raised livestock and gave free rein to slaughter. So whenever the prefectural or county authorities entered the mountains, those required to supply them were the temple monks, and the runners, relying on this, indulged their own appetites. What the superiors used was one part, but what came below was tenfold; thus the lives destroyed and the wealth spent in a year cannot be counted, and the temple's entanglements had no bottom. Moreover, those who came meant to bow to the Patriarch, yet fish and meat were spread before them — by no means a pure offering, nor the true intent of a benevolent man. The abuse was long accumulated and hard to reform. At first the Master was fortunate that Lord Zhou of Haimen, the surveillance commissioner, made a beginning of lifting the ban and permitted their petition; then Lord Yu, acting surveillance commissioner, strictly forbade slaughter, and the case was entered in the gazetteer. So whenever officials were to be supplied, the rule was a vegetarian pure offering — and this began when the Master entered the mountains. But he feared the dignity of the two offices would make it hard to enforce without fail. It happened that Lord Gu, the investigating censor, came into the mountains to pray for blessings for his parents, and the county pressed the monks as in the old manner. Lord Gu issued an order for fasting and precepts, and from then on it became a fixed rule. Once this was done, not only were lives protected and the pure rule made solemn, but expense was saved — a great sum reckoned by the year — and the community was spared bitter burden. The monks who kept the precepts advanced day by day, and the monastery was purified: all from this one act. Again the Master was graced by Lord Zhu, who came in person to the mountains to instruct the monks: keep the precepts, breed no livestock, kill nothing; turn the fish ponds into lotus pools. From this the mountain gate changed its face at once.
Clarifying the Rents to Benefit the Community

When the Master first entered the mountains, he looked over the community's annual accounts in the Patriarch's Hall and saw several sheets of contract notes, all of them loan agreements of the Patriarch's with interest at seven or eight parts in ten. The Master questioned him, and the supervising monk answered: the community's supplies were lacking, so we borrowed to meet them. The Master's heart ached at this. Then he asked the community: there were old incense-and-lamp estate fields; where do their rents go? He gathered the assembly to check thoroughly: for the Patriarch's incense and lamps there were the Bu-bo fields of Huangchao and Wengyuan, and the various estate fields acquired by the mountain since, totaling by the year about four hundred taels of rent. Where was it spent, that they should speak of shortage? The monks said: each estate, year by year, has simply been collected in turn by the managing monks of the ten quarters and spent by them. Looking into the cause, the managers and the tenant farmers were in collusion and cheating, so the rents fell into arrears and were never complete: an empty name with no real benefit, and the community grew daily poorer. The Master at once chose from the assembly ten monks who were upright, honest, and capable as managers, and had them swear before the Patriarch and write their pledge in their own blood, not to keep back a hair for themselves. He summoned the tenants of every estate and fixed the rules: each year a set time and a contract, payment to be brought to the temple. He established a treasury office and appointed four supervising stewards to manage the community's income and outlay. Then he reckoned every estate's annual rent in full, computed the total income, and drew up fixed rules for all the temple's expenditures, set down as a charter, leaving out not the smallest detail. After the outlay there was still a surplus. From this not only was the community well provided, but the Patriarch's Dharma-benefit spread like one rain moistening all alike, and the monks were no longer seeds for the hells. The pure rules and regulations are set out separately below. By imperial grant to the Nanhua Chan Temple of Caoxi, the community is established and the Long-Life Treasury revived; here follows the inscription on the clear regulations for the receipt and disbursement of money and grain.

When our Buddha, the World-Honored One, dwelt in the world, at first he led the assembly simply bearing their bowls and practicing the begging of food, and there was no accumulation at all — how could there be a community treasury? Later, because aged and sick monks could not go begging, he directed the monks who shared their dwelling to take half of what they had begged and bring it back for their support; this was called sharing the allotment, meaning to divide one's food and guard the work of the Way. The Vinaya texts record it in full. After the Buddha's nirvāṇa the practice in the Western Regions was no different from when he was alive. When the teaching flowed eastward, from the Yongping era of the Han down to the Tang, emperors, famous ministers, officials, and elders of successive dynasties each gave wealth to build temples and support monks as fields of merit. Yet often the temple heads abused it as their own, greedy and corrupt, destroying the Dharma and plundering the monks, and many feared no cause and effect. It was only with the Chan Master Baizhang, disciple of Mazu and heir of our Sixth Patriarch, that the pure rules were first created and the community treasury established. Within the monastery grounds, all offerings and profits, together with estate lands, money, and grain, had their appointed keepers. Hence the one who heads the temple is called the abbot, taking the preaching of Dharma as his charge and overseeing the general principles. Those who assist the monastery and help spread the Dharma's influence are the officers of the two sequences; such are the chief supervising steward and the supervising steward, who manage the community's treasury and are second to the abbot. The money and grain of the yearly accounts each have their storehouse for receipts and issues, and the office in charge is called the treasury office. From among the supervising stewards one of outstanding honesty is chosen to direct it; and lest his strength fall short, a deputy steward is appointed to assist him. For the estate lands there is an estate manager, and for collecting the rents there is a supervising collector. These are chosen from the assembly as men upright, honest, capable, generous, and forbearing. For those who handle disbursements there are the year steward and the month steward, who order the affairs of the mountain gate and receive officials and benefactors. Whenever anything is to be drawn or needed, it must be reported clearly to the abbot, the voucher approved and checked, and the treasury record plainly noted for later auditing. Thus not a hair's difference arises in the community's goods. So the monastery is like one body: the abbot is the head, the officers are the hands, feet, ears, and eyes, each needed by the others and not one to be lacking. Therefore in all the affairs of the mountain gate, when anything is to be done, high and low are of one mind, great and small of one strength, like eyes seeing, ears hearing, hands grasping, feet running — none fails to follow the command. That is why the monastery flourishes, the Dharma's influence prospers, outer insults do not invade, and inner hindrances do not arise. This is the model by which Buddhas and Patriarchs save the world, the standard of monasteries since ancient times.

Why is it that in recent ages the ancestral Way has declined and monasteries have fallen into ruin, while the instructions left by the sages are ignored in utter ignorance? Take our Sixth Patriarch's Caoxi: it is the source of the Chan school, its monastery the finest under heaven; its incense and offerings are no less than of old, yet the community treasury is ruined to the utmost, and the monks are foolish, deluded, and dull, not knowing what manner of thing it is. Because I spread the Dharma I met with calamity and was graced with exile beyond the range. In the second month of spring in the bing-shen year of Wanli I bowed to the Sixth Patriarch and saw his Dharma-bones, solemn as if alive, while the mountain gate was so desolate it was scarcely fit to look upon; I paced and wept for a long while. Moreover the monks, set upon by the courts and dragged about, were pressed as urgently as sparks from flint, hounded day and night, until more than half had ruined their families and sold their property, so that the ancestral courtyard fell into decay and was nearly swept from the earth. Fortunately the Commander-in-Chief Lord Chen showed some forbearance toward them; then Lord Zhou of the Salt and Grain Circuit, acting at Nan-Shao, somewhat reformed the abuse of supplying officials with wine and meat; then Lord Zhu of Nan-Shao severely punished the monks' faults and, forbidding the breeding of livestock and slaughter, strove to save them. He directed the whole mountain's monks to press me again and again to enter the mountains and set matters in order. In the winter of the ji-hai year, the twenty-seventh of Wanli, Lord Zhu charged me earnestly to my face. In the first month of spring the next year, geng-zi, he again sent the temple monks Zhenquan, Xingyu, Jingtai, Huishan, Yuanshi, and others with letters to Wuyang to urge me into the mountains. As I was then in the camp I had no leisure to accept. In the fourth month Lord Zhu went north to offer congratulations; I saw him off at Lingzhou, and he did me the honor of repeating his charge face to face. In the ninth month of that autumn I at last took my staff and entered the mountains. Once there, I first chose a number of monks and gave them the full precepts; together we gathered in the halls twice a day and recited the Lotus Sutra. Next I chose a number of novices fit to be taught and had them study the scriptures, dividing them into three studies, and chose from the assembly those of somewhat superior learning and conduct as teachers. Next I surveyed the general fengshui of the mountain gate: whatever clashed, injured, or overcame I removed; whatever was broken I repaired. I closed the gate of the spirit source, banked up the elephant's trunk to strengthen the ancestral courtyard, opened the road at the mountain gate, and moved the stone archway so as to receive the primal energy. Within three months all was transformed with one accord. Now inside the mountain gate, drifters had long been hiding, seizing the temple's foundations, opening shops, wine-houses, and butchers' stalls, setting cunning snares of lewdness and gambling, colluding with local villains, swindling and harming the temple monks, fierce as jackals and tigers. Habit had made it a custom, entrenched beyond dislodging, a great poison and a hidden grief to me. In the twelfth month of that year I went again to Duanzhou to pay my respects to the Commander-in-Chief Lord Dai and asked for an order to drive them out. Presently the order went down to Qujiang, with a limit of three days to drive them all beyond the border, allowing not one man or one shop to remain. Thereupon the villains vanished, and the temple foundations and market streets they had seized all returned to the community. I then blocked off the east-west passage through the center; on the left of the great road I set up an official residence as a resting place for travelers from Wengyuan and elsewhere, inscribed Three Lives Come; on the right I set up the Pilgrims' Lodge of the Ten Directions to welcome monks from every quarter as a place to hang their staffs, inscribed One Night's Awakening. I moved the thoroughfare to the streamside, so that travelers coming and going were each properly accommodated and no longer mixed in confusion. From this the monastery was clean and the monks slept in peace. On the third day of the first month of spring in the next year, xin-chou, I received the Commander-in-Chief's summons and went to Qingying on local business, and further begged Lord Li, the eunuch commissioner, to be the benefactor of the revival. In the seventh month Lord Li entered the mountains to bow to the Patriarch and gladly gave three hundred taels toward rebuilding the mountain gate. Then I directed the temple monks to examine in full the estate rents for the Sixth Patriarch's offerings and incense and lamps. What was gained each year had never, by a hair, entered the community treasury; all had been plundered by the keepers, and this had become the custom. So I first set in order the rents of the Taiping estate, and had the tax silver for the twenty-ninth year of Wanli already entered into the community treasury, with the three periods of spring, autumn, and winter fixed so that it might be spent in the current year. Now I brought in as well the Bu-bo fields of Huangchao and Wanshan and the various estates acquired by the temple since, all to be collected in advance and spent in the following year. Besides completing in advance the rents of the twenty-ninth year from those estates, from the thirtieth year on this was made the fixed rule. I further examined that the temple formerly had a Long-Life Treasury, and now revived it: all the community's rents and the benefactors' money and grain were to be stored in the treasury, and following the pure rules and precedents, officers were appointed — four supervising stewards to manage receipts and disbursements, chosen from the assembly as men mature, honest, and capable. The temple's ten quarters formerly had one chief manager and nine stewards, whose duty was to serve the corvée, welcome officials, supply the prefecture and county, and procure pepper, tea, palm, fruit, and bamboo shoots; yet the community's rents had all been swallowed up by these men — bitterly hateful. Now ten monks of experience and understanding were chosen to fill these posts. All things needed were apportioned by head; each monk contributed a little, taken in advance into the treasury to meet the superiors' unforeseen needs, thus sparing trouble and harassment. The rents received into the treasury from each estate were to be drawn and paid according to the regular law of land tax and corvée, in exact amount, without arrears or fraudulent shortfall. The cost of receiving officials who enter the mountains was given fixed rules, so that the officers were not unevenly burdened. The incense and lamp offerings of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' halls each had their fixed scale, so that the intent of offering and repaying the root was not lost. The officers who run about all year in hardship were also given their reward, so that toil and ease were equal and no complaints arose. The completeness or shortfall of rents collected was assessed, and the amounts raised or lowered accordingly, to make diligence and idleness plain. The four items above were all disbursed from the treasury. Only the tuition for teaching the novices — apart from the Confucian teacher, whom I provided for myself — came from the stupa fund, drawing down on the Patriarch's robe and bowl to train the novices and increase the shame of the young; this too had its fixed rule. In this way the community's money and grain had no channel of waste, the keepers and officers had no crack for self-theft, the monks had no cause for vexation, and the community could be a plan for the long term. Moreover all the monks of the temple, great and small, were given the precepts, to avoid the reproach of disgracing the ancestral courtyard and to spare the cost of wine and meat as provision for clothing and food. Thus when clothing and food suffice, propriety and righteousness arise, and this defiled land can be turned into a pure Buddha-land.
Itemized: 1. The Appointment of Officers

Four supervising stewards, solely in charge of the treasury office, receiving and disbursing the community's money and grain, procuring supplies, and directing the great affairs of the mountain gate, second to the abbot. All matters are to be discussed and settled with one mind. Of these, one is solely in charge of the keys, managing the receipt and storage of all money, grain, and goods, so that responsibility is fixed. Another supervises the collection of rents, reporting and impeaching abuses so that they do not spread, and serves as the assembly's discipline. A secretary of the treasury office is appointed to keep the registers of receipts and disbursements for auditing, so that nothing is missed. One household chief: this follows the old rule, in charge of the ward levies, corvée, and grain taxes, still according to the regular practice; this is the ancient deputy steward. One chief manager: this post is the ancient chief administrator, head of the administrators; now this post is combined with that of estate manager, leading the stewards in collecting the rents of each estate and urging on the grain levies and corvée of the whole temple, second to the household chief; he is also called the year steward. Nine stewards of the ninth grade: these are the ancient administrators, assisting the chief manager in collecting grain levies and corvée, taking turns as month steward, receiving officials, and managing the great and small affairs of the mountain gate. These ten officers now follow the old rule of the temple's ten quarters, each quarter serving in turn, changed at the year's end. Hence formerly these posts went to worthless men, who mostly could not manage great affairs. Now men of outstanding ability are specially chosen to fill them. When the time of year-end replacement comes, the abbot and supervising stewards are still to look for those of outstanding worth and toil and keep them on as before; those unfit, or who for other reasons cannot serve, are replaced by men chosen for honesty, capacity, and maturity. If any do not keep the pure rules, defy the law and follow private interest, or collude with the tenants to ruin the community and leave rents in arrears, or covet small gains and fleece the tenant farmers and exploit the monks, to the injury of the general good, the chief manager and supervising stewards must not conceal it, but report at once to the abbot; the bell is struck and the assembly gathered, and before the Patriarch his crime is plainly proved. For a light offense he is punished in due measure and dismissed, and another capable man chosen in his place without waiting for the year's end; for a grave offense he is handed over to the authorities and dealt with by law, as a warning to the rest. Nor may the abbot indulge him out of private feeling, so as to breed a great harm. Be careful, be careful.

1. Clarifying Receipts and Disbursements. There are five categories of receipt: the annual offerings and profits of the Patriarch's Hall, together with silver caps and vessels; the annual rents of the community's estates; the donations of officials who enter the mountains and of benefactors who rejoice in giving, and all that is raised for building and repairs and for feeding the monks; fines imposed on offending monks, together with money, grain, incense, and oil entering the community and the silver and goods from official quarters, properties, and fields that should come in; and the value of materials bought back from the treasury, the goods of deceased monks that should revert to the community, and the deeds of fields, houses, and goods purchased by the community. Each has its own heading and is set out one by one, entered in the registers for auditing.

For each category two receipt ledgers are kept, one held by the abbot and one by the treasury office. Whatever is to be received is received in the Patriarch's Hall before the assembly. Each estate's annual rent has its upper and lower time limits; before the time, the chief manager leads the stewards in urging all the tenants, holding the field chiefs responsible, until the silver is collected in full and brought in person to the Patriarch's Hall, to be handed over and weighed before the abbot and supervising stewards. The supervising collector holds the balance even, checks the weighing plainly, the secretary enters it in the ledger, and the abbot seals it. Then from the treasury a printed receipt is taken, matched with the abbot's receipt ledger, the amount written in, the tally seal stamped across the join, and each officer signs his mark below his own title; only then is it given to the field chief as the warrant. The officers may not issue it privately. If on inspection a rent proves to have no printed receipt, it is collusion and fraud against the abbot; the heads must report it and send the man to the authorities to be punished by law. In the two seasons of spring and autumn, when benefactors of the ten directions come before the Patriarch to offer incense and present silver caps, flower vessels, silver, robes, and other goods, the stupa keeper collects them item by item and the abbot enters them in the ledger. At the year's end, at the time of replacement, the totals are reckoned and the figures plainly examined. What should be kept is stored as before; what the Patriarch's Hall needs is handed over to the treasury and received and spent by the rule. At the time, the elders of the assembly must be gathered to examine it together; the stupa keeper may not conceal anything or join with the officers in shielding one another. If this is found out, he is punished as one who has embezzled public goods. All donations by officials, and all money and grain raised for building and repairs, for feeding monks, and for rice, and indeed everything that belongs to the community, is entered in ledgers by the rule, item by item, and received according to law; nothing may be hidden or omitted. If anything that should be received is not entered in the ledger, the secretary and supervising stewards are held guilty of collusion and fraud. For all disbursements of silver, grain, and goods, the month steward and stewards write out a voucher by the rule and first present it to the abbot for approval; when the abbot permits it, the voucher is copied into the disbursement ledger, numbered in sequence, and the amount to be drawn written in two places, sealed across the join with a private seal, and the words approved for drawing written in the blank space. The month steward in charge takes the voucher to the treasury and draws the amount; the treasury secretary copies the voucher into the disbursement ledger, and only then may the supervising steward issue the silver in the stated amount. Without the sealed and numbered voucher it is an unauthorized drawing: if small, the man is punished in due measure before the Patriarch and the assembly; if large, he is sent to the authorities to be dealt with by law. Should it not be for public use, and the abbot out of private feeling, together with the month steward and the keepers, issue a false voucher and draw out money or goods, whatever the amount, once found out it is treated as the supervising collector's own theft. The Long-Life Treasury is set up solely to hold savings, the place where the supervising stewards manage money and grain; many may not intrude there. Hence the stewards' quarters are also set up as a place of meeting. Whenever a month steward is on duty, the managing monk must dwell solely in those quarters for the month, overseeing all the community's affairs within and without; the money, grain, and goods spent are reckoned plainly at the month's end and written into a monthly report booklet sent to the abbot, who checks it plainly and writes the two words no error, then sends it to the treasury office for the year-end summary, so that nothing is confused. At the year's end, on the first day of the tenth month, the time of replacement, the abbot gathers the assembly beforehand to settle the year's accounts of receipt and disbursement. On that day the supervising stewards, the secretary, and the chief managers of the ten quarters each bring their ledgers and gather together in the Patriarch's Hall. Elders able to reckon are invited, one to handle the counting and one to call out the figures, and before the assembly they reckon it plainly together; the whole is given to the secretary, who draws up the record, setting out: in such a year this temple's community received in all so much rent in money and grain, so much in donations, such and such goods; now such items and miscellaneous items have been spent to such an amount, there remains such an amount, and perhaps such an amount of rent is still in arrears — all set out item by item. A general register is made in four identical copies: one sent to the Patriarch's Hall and stored in its case, one sent to the revival community, and one left with the treasury office, as a permanent standard. Pepper, tea, palm, and fruit are all treated in the same way. The fixed annual items of expenditure are set out below.

Itemized: there are fifteen categories. Payment of grain levies and corvée: according to the land, by the rule, each year roughly a hundred taels and more; if land is newly added or an intercalary month brings extra corvée, it increases but does not decrease; if tax exemption is granted, it decreases but does not increase. Incense and lamps for the Buddha Hall: ten taels a year.
Offerings of incense and lamps for the Patriarch's Hall: fifty taels a year.

For the Dharma-protecting deities, offerings on the first and fifteenth of every month: twelve taels a year in all; in an intercalary month, none. For the abbot's reception of superiors and officials passing through: formerly eleven taels a year, with four added. For the household chief's reception of officials: formerly ten taels a year, with two added.

Four supervising stewards and one treasury secretary: each three taels six mace a year for their meals, eighteen taels in all. The chief manager and nine stewards, ten men: each three taels six mace a year for meals, thirty-six taels in all. One newly appointed mountain warden, to watch over the trees of the ancestral mountain and tend and plant them: a measured allowance of one tael five mace a year for rice. Six sutra-keepers and chant leaders, who daily lead the assembly in recitation in the various halls: each given two bolts of cloth, reckoned at five mace of silver, three taels in all. Two old attendants and one servant, to watch over the official residence, strike the bell and drum, and announce guests, and to serve the community's errands and duties: each one tael two mace a year for board and wages, three taels six mace in all. For the revival of the ancestral courtyard and the rebuilding of the Wujin Hermitage, thirty taels a year are set aside for offerings and incense; this is beyond the regular items, having been provided from the offerings and profits the Patriarch himself received, and is not to be compared with what others have given. Those who later preside, use, or manage it must not treat it lightly, lest they bring grave guilt upon themselves. Be careful, be careful. From the thirty-fourth year, when the Chan Hall was built, this silver was put into the hall for the use of the community of the ten directions in feeding the assembly, and has nothing to do with the hermitage. Whenever the two offices of the governor and censor enter the mountains, apart from the three posts of stupa keeper, abbot, and household chief, which receive the superiors, all other officials — prefectural, county, military, inspecting, garrison, merit-awarding, central army, company commanders, guard and battalion, and constables — and ordinary superiors' messengers and runners are still entertained by the ten quarters in turn according to the old rule, and may not be charged to the community's account.
For comings and goings to and from Wengyuan county, the month steward is solely responsible; the fixed rules for receiving them and providing meals are these.
The chief magistrate: one mace of silver for each meal. The assistant and subordinate officials: seven fen of silver for each meal.
The Confucian school officials: five fen of silver for each meal. The clerks: three fen of silver for each meal.

For the four items above, once the steward has received the guests he writes a voucher, takes it to the abbot for sealing, and draws the amount from the treasury. If the guest is not of this county, the old rule still applies.
For teaching the novices the scriptures: three teachers, ten taels a year in all, and two bolts of cloth each, each bolt reckoned at two mace five fen of silver. All this is drawn

from the Patriarch's robe and bowl, provided by the stupa keeper of the year. Besides this, each man is given a pair of shoes, reckoned at two mace of silver, paid from the community treasury. If the Patriarch's Hall has nothing to give, it is drawn from the Long-Life Treasury in the same manner as the supervising stewards, paid year by year and not in driblets. The meals they are provided, following the number of the Chan Hall assembly, are as in the rules above; the ancestral incense-and-lamp estate rents are still apportioned and shared in common for the public use, as a fixed standard forever. Those who later are abbots, heads, or officers may not conceive a thought of greed to devour the community, or follow private feeling and capriciously increase or decrease. Even when each year's ancestral rents are fully collected, if after the above outlays there is still surplus, the officers may not cunningly devise pretexts or invent new categories to draw on it at will. Only repair of the mountain gate, the travel expenses of officers going out and coming in, and matters of the community's common use that cannot be avoided may be drawn. Let each man be sparing, and keep in mind the enriching of the community; never harbor a thought of seeking petty gain and so bring hell upon himself. The ancient worthies said: in the community's goods, if the abbot and those who manage receipts and disbursements can skillfully reduce wasteful expense, then money and grain become inexhaustible. From this, year by year, savings accumulate, management follows the rule, and it grows and flourishes month by month: no monastery can fail to prosper, no Dharma-wheel fail to turn. I received the Patriarch's charge to mend what was toppling and prop up the fallen order — no small matter. You officers must keep to it, not slighting it by a hair. Alas, keep it in mind. The community's goods are weighty in the smallest particle, for they are the benefactors' seeds in the field of merit, the fat and blood of their faith; how could one lightly deceive and steal them? The ancient worthies said: the community's goods are almost like pigeon poison — touch one grain and your liver splits, your head shatters, your whole body rots. So all who manage and hold office, if they know cause and effect, are thereby building heavenly palaces and Pure Lands; those who do not know cause and effect are building immeasurable hells, with iron beds, copper pillars, and blazing iron balls, and misery for ten thousand kalpas — and not only the debt of wearing horns and fur, bearing iron and saddles, to repay old debts. Moreover the king's law is stern and the gods observe; should one not fear? Let every officer of mine examine himself earnestly. Think on it, keep it in mind.
